figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of the network architecture and plasticity mechanisms. (a) The network consists of three layers: the input, recurrent, and action-selection layer. The recurrent layer includes excitatory (blue dots) and inhibitory (red dots) populations. Only a subset of connections are indicated to illustrate the connectivity. (b) Recurrent connectivity kernels. Excitatory (red) and inhibitory (black) neurons receiving connections from a central excitatory (left plot) and inhibitory (right plot) neuron. (c) Symmetric STDP kernel (d) Weight normalization scheme used for synaptic normalization.

Figure 2: Bifurcation diagram and network activity across the operating parameter regime. (a) Homogeneous bifurcation (k = 0) diagram of the network dynamics in the plane of W eff IE = WIE ( V E R − Vth ) and W eff EE = WEE ( V E R − Vth ) , where V E R denotes the excitatory synaptic reversal potential. Saddle-node bifurcations on the low, middle, and high firing branches of the nullclines are shown as blue lines, the Hopf bifurcation as a red line, and the Bogdanov–Takens point (at the intersection of the saddle-node and Hopf bifurcation lines) is marked with black dots. The dashed line indicates a saddle homoclinic bifurcation. (b) Excitatory and inhibitory nullclines, along with population excitatory rates, are shown for the regions indicated on the bifurcation diagram. (c) Network activity in response to a pulse input applied to neurons at the center. (d) Spontaneous activity driven by uncorrelated noise.

Figure 3: Burst characteristics when the network is tuned to the edge of instability, near the Bogdanov–Takens bifurcation point (System No.1 in the bifurcation map) (a) Instantaneous excitatory versus inhibitory activity, binned in 5 ms intervals; (b,c) Distribution of burst sizes (b) and burst durations (c). (d) Average size vs. average burst duration. (e) Temporal profiles of three bursts with different durations (T ) are shown. The time axis is normalized by the total duration (t/T ), and the amplitude is scaled by T 1−γ . The collapse onto a single universal curve indicates self-similar dynamics across scales. (f) The best-fit exponent γ for the shape collapse was determined by minimizing the variance score (mean squared residual) across the rescaled temporal profiles.

Figure 4: Turing Bifurcation and Pattern Formation. (a) Bifurcation map illustrating the onset of Turing instabilities alongside saddle-node and Hopf bifurcations of the mean-field equation. The parameter space is defined by the relative kernel widths (β) and amplitudes (α) of the excitatory (Exc.) and inhibitory (Inh.) populations. The Hopf and Turing bifurcation lines intersect at a Hopf-Turing point, where oscillatory patterns emerge. Note that while the exact transition points in the 2D spatial system are shifted relative to the mean-field approximation, the qualitative structure of the map remains valid. (b) Network population rates for five representative examples of excitatory weight kernel widths and amplitudes. (c) Snapshots of spatial activity patterns taken at 10 ms intervals. (d) Dispersion curves for a fixed width ratio β = σE/σI = 0.75 and varying amplitude ratios α = AE/AI . The onset of Turing instability occurs at α = 1.19 for the mode k = 1.24. (e) Thresholds for Turing and Hopf onsets as a function of α at a fixed β. (f) Effective weight kernels for the three networks corresponding to the numbered locations in panels (a) and (b).

Figure 5: Learning a shortcut path via preplay during navigation. (a) Successive trajectories during active exploration: left, the previously learned non-optimal path; middle and right, trajectories selected by the agent using preplay of future states and actions. (b) Snapshots of network activity at a location along the non-optimal path (indicated in the left trajectory plot) over a 75 ms time window, showing activity propagating toward the reward location. (c) Shift of the activity bump on the ring attractor in the direction corresponding to the vector average of upcoming actions. (d) Action direction at each location along the path, shown while the agent occupies each point for an interval of 75 ms. (e) Activity propagation along the newly formed line attractor; the previous attractor is suppressed by the new assembly and downscaled via synaptic normalization. (f) Vector average of connections from place cells to action cells, drawn at the spatial location of each cell’s peak firing. (g) Maps of recurrent connectivity: (top left) WEE after learning the non-optimal path; (top right) WEE after learning the optimal path; (bottom panels) corresponding maps for WIE .

Figure 6: Forward and Backward Replay. (a) Effective average synaptic weight from a point along the chain to its neighbors at distance r, Weff(r). (b–d) Forward and backward wave propagation when the agent is located at the beginning, middle, and end of the path. Top panels: Average firing rates of neurons when the agent is at a particular location at the end of learning. Bottom panels: Replay activity of selected neurons along the path during six successive learning trials when the agent is at the corresponding locations. Red and blue dashed line indicate samples of forward and backward sequence replay, respectively. Learning strengthens inner connections and stabilizes replay activity. When the agent is in the middle of the path, forward wave propagation becomes dominant, prioritized, and more frequent.

Figure 7: Influence of Distinct Spontaneous Dynamic Activity States on Sequence Replay (a1) The sequence embedded as a directed neuronal chain. (a2) Activity propagation during exploration along this path forms an attractor (a3) within the network. (b1) Network activity and spike raster of neurons in the chain when the network is in a homogeneous irregular firing state. (b2) Same for the synchronous irregular (population bursting) state. (b3) Same as (b2), but after the network has undergone synaptic reconfiguration corresponding to (a3) during exploration. (c1–3) Overall heatmaps of neuronal activity for the networks in (b2) and (b3), respectively. (d1-3) Chain weight change (in percentage) for those networks. (e) Change in synaptic weights of a chain with various initial average weights after 30 s of simulation under different network states. (f) Rate of chain activation for a fixed initial normalized weight during 60 s of simulation.

Figure 8: Effect of replay in reducing latency and stabilizing the path to the goal. (a) Two exploration trials before and after offline replay. The middle plots show neural activity during rest, indicating increased activity in place cells that encode the previously explored path and demonstrating the effect of replay on the action encoded for each location. (b)Average effect of offline replay on latency (top plot) and success rate (bottom plot) during exploration. Results are shown for multiple sequences of explorations, each consisting of six trials starting from the first successful trial in which the agent reaches the goal. During active exploration, internal noise can destabilize the trajectory, causing the agent to miss the goal within the maximum trial duration in subsequent trials. Replay-driven consolidation strengthens the learned path and improves navigation stability. (c) Effect of offline replay after different numbers of successful explorations. (Top) Example case; (Middle) average and variance of trial times across 20 such experiments; (Bottom) same as above, but trial times are normalized by the earliest successful exploration trial time.

Figure 9: Effect of Learning Rules on Network Dynamics and Task Performance. (a) (Left) Radial balance condition before path learning, indicating weak dominance of local inhibition. (Middle) Effect of spike-timing–dependent plasticity (STDP) in excitatory-to-inhibitory (E → I) connections on maintaining excitation–inhibition balance. (Right) Role of synaptic normalization in shaping a metastable attractor along the rewarded path. (b) Exploration behavior following replay periods, with and without synaptic normalization. (c) Probability of a successful trial conditioned on the success of the previous trial under three conditions: exploration without excitation–inhibition balance, rest without synaptic normalization, and rest with synaptic normalization.

Figure 10: Diffusive Offline Replay After Foraging Task (a) Trajectory during the foraging task. (b) Population firing organized into bursts of varying sizes. (c) Decoded positions during two example bursts. Neural activity is binned in 5 ms intervals, and positions are decoded using a weighted average of place-cell firing rates. (d) Log–log plot of distance versus time for all bursts. (e) Mean (top) and standard deviation (bottom) of effective radial weight profiles (WEE on the left and WIE on the right) from a center neuron to its postsynaptic targets at distance r, averaged over multiple locations in the environment before foraging, after foraging, and after offline replay with synaptic normalization.

Figure 11: Effect of replay in generalization of the place to action map.(a) The top panel shows three successive exploration trials. The corresponding action maps during these exploration phases are displayed in the second row. In one experiment, the network undergoes diffusive replay, while in the other it does not; the starting point is then changed, and exploration is run for both cases. (b) Same experiment as in (a), but performed over ten independent runs. In each run, the effect of replay is compared to no replay after [1, 3, 5, 7] successful exploration trials.

Figure A.1: Bump formation and integration on the ring attractor network. (a) Integration, coexistence, and competition of activity bumps on a ring attractor. (b) Top: Network activity in response to two inputs of equal strength applied at a 90° separation. Bottom: Corresponding excitatory connectivity kernels for each network. (c) Illustration of how multiple inputs facilitate bump integration and how input separation affects the width of the integrated bump. (d) Network response to three inputs separated by 90°, presented on top of background noise. A high level of background noise can amplify small input fluctuations and promote the formation of an integrated bump.

Figure A.2: Approximation of the neuronal gain function in response to Poisson input. (a) Average membrane potential, its variance, and firing rate of the neuron model under various fixed external inhibitory rates (each color corresponds to a different inhibition level) and varying excitation. Dashed lines represent analytical results, and solid lines show simulation data. (b) Top: Three networks maintained at constant membrane potential by applying balanced excitatory–inhibitory input rates as shown in the top graph (the E–I relationship is linear). Middle: Membrane potential variance under balanced input; at higher balanced rates, both variance and firing rate decrease. Bottom: Output rate and self-consistency curve for balanced homogeneous solutions in the network.

Table 2: Comparison of critical exponents in the oscillatory critical model against the directed percolation universality class. MF-Br: mean-field branching process (DP universality class). 2D-DP: two-dimensional directed percolation. Local+LR: local 2D excitation with sparse long-range connections, the network analyzed in the main text (Fig. 3, System No. 1, near the Bogdanov–Takens point). Rand-MF: purely random, sparse network with mean-field-like connectivity, analyzed in this appendix. 2D-Latt: purely local 2D lattice network, analyzed in this appendix.

Figure A.3: Scale-Free Bursts in Random and Strictly Local Networks. a) Schematic of postsynaptic excitatory (red) and inhibitory (black) neurons connected to central excitatory neurons. Top: Random network; Bottom: Locally connected network. b) Burst detection methodology: events are defined by network activity exceeding a threshold determined by the background firing rate under external input. c) Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function (CCDF) of burst sizes with a fitted power law. d) CCDF of burst durations with a fitted power law. e) Average burst size vs. duration (lifetime) with a fitted power-law scaling relationship.

Figure A.4: Total input and firing rate covariances between neurons in distinct dynamical regimes (a) Temporal profiles of average excitation, inhibition, and their difference across all bursts (normalized by burst duration). (b) (Left) Cross-correlations between neurons total input at various spatial distances, measured at different time points within the normalized burst. (Right) same when network is set at homogeneous firing state, normalized by total simulation time. (c) System in a critical regime with scale-free avalanches: (c-1) Spatial firing rate correlations of neurons as a function of distance, calculated across various time bin sizes with power-law fits. (c-2) Raster plot of neurons firing along a chain (nodes distributed randomly over the spatial domain) alongside the total population activity. (c-3) Synaptic changes via STDP along the chain after 50 s of simulation. (d) Same as (c) but for a system showing non-critical, locally confined bursts: (d-1) The spatial correlation function decays exponentially. (d-2) Raster plot of neuron chains shows less synchronous activation across the chain. (d-3) Synaptic changes via STDP are weaker due to the absence of long-range correlations.

Figure A.5: Interaction of two neuronal sequences in scale-free and locally confined bursting regimes. (a) Embedding of the neural sequences through active exploration of two straight paths. (b-1) Raster plot of sequence replay and population firing rate in the network with locally confined bursts. (b-2) Same as (b1) for the network with scale-free bursts.(c-1 and c-2) Firing rate maps of neurons during spontaneous activity for the two systems. (d-1) Synaptic weight changes between neurons for existing connections in the network with locally confined bursts. (d-2) Same for the network with scale-free bursts.

Figure A.6: Effect of the spontaneous firing regime on behavioral performance. (a) Left: a learned trajectory after exploration and before the replay period. Middle: spontaneous firing rates in the three regimes (hyperexcitable, balanced and overinhibited). Right: the effect of replay on the action encoded at each spatial location, and the resulting behavioral trajectory after replay. (b) Mean percentage change in trial time after replay, computed over 15 different non-optimal trajectories, for the hyperexcitable (HE), balanced (BAL) and overinhibited (OI) regimes. Error bars show the variance across trajectories.

Figure A.7: Transient diffusion in an E–I network on a ring. (a) Firing rates of 20 excitatory populations over time. (b) Overall average network firing rate and individual firing rates for selected populations. (c) Decoded trajectory of the phase θ for the largest burst event, calculated using weighted and unweighted averages of population activity. (d) Mean squared displacement ⟨θ2(t)⟩ as a function of time, characterizing the diffusive (random walk) nature of the decoded phase.
